title: THE COMPANY THAT SELLS YOU NOTHING — ENGINE BEAT SCRIPT

beats.name: COLD OPEN / STRANGE OBSERVATION
beats.vo: Planet Fitness ended 2025 with about twenty point eight million members. It had two thousand eight hundred and ninety-six clubs.
beats.visual: EXACT EMPTY PLANET FITNESS-STYLE GYM AT 4:00 A.M.; wide locked-off shot, fluorescent hum, machines clean, nobody there.
beats.question: How can a gym support that many members?
beats.reveal: The audience sees the impossible scale before the mechanism is explained.
beats.hook: THE COMPANY THAT SELLS YOU NOTHING

beats.name: THE IMPOSSIBLE RATIO
beats.vo: That is roughly seven thousand two hundred members for every location. Four percent of those members would be about eight hundred and thirty thousand people. And that is the point. The business is not built for everybody to show up. It is built around the opposite possibility.
beats.visual: Membership count → club count → 7,200 ratio → occupancy mismatch; then return to the empty gym with one tiny treadmill user.
beats.question: What if low attendance is not a failure?
beats.reveal: The business depends on most members not consuming capacity.

beats.name: THE PERFECT CUSTOMER
beats.vo: Because the member who never walks through this door is not necessarily a failed customer. They may be the perfect one. The trick is not the contract. It is the friction.
beats.visual: Empty room → distant inactive member slot → subtle transition to a recurring bank charge.
beats.question: Why would friction be the product?
beats.reveal: The story shifts from fitness to recurring-payment psychology.

beats.name: THE $86 / $219 GAP
beats.vo: Here's the number that makes the gym make sense. When researchers asked a thousand Americans to estimate their monthly subscription spending, the average answer was eighty-six dollars. Then the same people were forced to itemize the charges: streaming, music, cloud storage, the gym, the app downloaded for a trip two years ago. The average was two hundred and nineteen. One hundred and thirty-three dollars a month higher than people thought. A hundred and thirty-three dollars is not a rounding error. It is sixteen hundred dollars a year.
beats.visual: Bank statement. $86 appears alone → black hold → $219 replaces it → $133 isolates → annual $1,600 appears after a pause.
beats.question: How does a payment become background noise?
beats.reveal: Recurring payments create a gap between remembered spending and actual spending.

beats.name: THE PATTERN SPREADS
beats.vo: And the reason this matters is not that people are bad at arithmetic. It is that recurring payments are designed to become background noise. That gap is where the business model starts. Once one company discovered it could get paid for a service a customer barely used, the idea was portable. Another industry copied it. Then another. This is not one company's trick. It is a pattern.
beats.visual: Recurring charges repeat down statement → charge fades into noise → one industry card becomes several industry cards.
beats.question: Where did the pattern begin?
beats.reveal: The story is about a system, not a single company.

beats.name: GYM ECONOMICS
beats.vo: Start with the gym, because the gym makes the economics visible without hiding behind software. A gym has a strange cost structure. The building costs the same whether one person walks in or a thousand do. The machines cost the same. The lease, the lights, the insurance, the staff at the desk — most of it exists whether the customer arrives tonight or not. So an extra member can be extraordinarily cheap — until that member actually appears. Then they need a machine. A shower. Floor space. Staff time. The economics flip the instant the customer consumes the thing they bought.
beats.visual: Cost line flat → revenue line rises → second cost-to-serve line stays flat then spikes at real usage.
beats.question: What kind of member creates the best economics?
beats.reveal: Capacity, not membership, is the scarce resource.

beats.name: THE MEMBER WHO DOESN'T CONSUME
beats.vo: So the ideal customer is not mysterious. It is the customer who pays — and does not consume. Industry estimates have put the share of gym memberships that go essentially unused at up to two-thirds. That is an industry estimate, not an audited universal number, but the direction matters. People intend to go. Most people intended to go in January.
beats.visual: Empty machines → January gym-search spike → February collapse → calendar advances while membership charge continues.
beats.question: What is this revenue called?
beats.reveal: Human intention becomes part of the economics.

beats.name: BREAKAGE
beats.vo: There is a word for revenue a company collects for a service it never has to deliver. Breakage. The word came out of the gift-card business.
beats.visual: Black field → single word BREAKAGE → gift card appears.
beats.question: How is subscription breakage different from a gift card?
beats.reveal: The mechanism receives a name.

beats.name: ONE TIME VS EVERY MONTH
beats.vo: A card gets bought, partly spent, thrown in a drawer, and the unused balance eventually becomes revenue that cost almost nothing to fulfill. Airlines have versions of it with expired miles. Retailers have it with store credit. But a gift card breaks once. A subscription is different. It can break again next month. And the month after that. And the month after that — until somebody actively interrupts the payment.
beats.visual: Gift card fades once → calendar cards continue below frame → same recurring charge repeats indefinitely.
beats.question: What does recurring forgetting become?
beats.reveal: Forgetting can become recurring revenue.

beats.name: FORGETTING AS REVENUE
beats.vo: That changes the value of forgetting. For a subscription company, forgetting is not a one-time accident. It is recurring revenue.
beats.visual: Recurring charge repeats down a long vertical bank statement; older charges fade into background noise.
beats.question: If that works, why did older gyms use hard contracts?
beats.reveal: The model's weakness becomes the next story problem.

beats.name: BALLY / THE OLD MODEL
beats.vo: The first companies to industrialise this got it wrong, and the way they got it wrong is instructive. Through the nineties, the dominant American gym chain was Bally. Its model leaned on long contracts and hard cancellation terms. Customers described short-term offers turning into much longer obligations, billing disputes, and cancellations that did not behave the way the customer expected. Federal and state regulators investigated aspects of the company's billing and cancellation practices at different points in the 1990s and 2000s. Bally settled those matters and agreed to reforms.
beats.visual: 1990s Bally storefront → membership desk → contract close-up → complaint forms → regulator documents.
beats.question: Why did the contract become a liability?
beats.reveal: The visible trap creates an identifiable aggrieved customer.

beats.name: COMPLAINTS / WRONG WEAPON
beats.vo: Now read what happened next as a product-design lesson. Bally's model extracted money from customers who had stopped attending. But it also created something dangerous. It created a victim with a document. A customer could point at the contract and say: I tried to leave. That produces complaints. Complaints produce attorneys general. Attorneys general produce settlements. So the next generation removed the weapon that created the complaints: the obvious contract.
beats.visual: Contract → customer complaint → attorney general → settlement → black field with THE CONTRACT WAS THE WRONG WEAPON.
beats.text: THE CONTRACT WAS THE WRONG WEAPON
beats.question: What replaces the visible contract?
beats.reveal: Friction becomes the replacement.

beats.name: PLANET FITNESS / FRICTION
beats.vo: Planet Fitness will let you cancel. There is no three-year term sitting on the screen waiting to be escaped. And that is exactly why the business model gets more interesting. You do not need a three-year trap if leaving costs twenty irritated minutes.
beats.visual: Bright, friendly Planet Fitness-style storefront → generic login → password reset → retention screen → confirmation.
beats.question: Can a low price make leaving feel irrational?
beats.reveal: Friction can replace a visible contractual trap.

beats.name: $10 VS $99
beats.vo: And there is an even smarter piece. If you want to maximise breakage, a very high price can be the wrong tool. Charge ninety-nine dollars a month and the customer notices. It appears on the statement like a problem. Charge ten dollars and the psychology changes. Ten dollars is not free. But cancelling it can require a login, a password reset, a retention screen, and the irritating question: why are you leaving? Twenty minutes of friction to recover ten dollars.
beats.visual: $99 statement line obvious → $10 line among many charges → cancellation path implied.
beats.question: Why does stopping feel more expensive than continuing?
beats.reveal: Time and attention become hidden cancellation costs.

beats.name: THE INTENTION PRODUCT
beats.vo: Most people do the same mental calculation without writing it down. They keep paying. Not because they cannot afford to stop. Because stopping feels like work. The gym is not selling you fitness. It is selling the intention to become the person who goes. And then it bills you for the gap between that intention and your Tuesday evening.
beats.visual: Empty gym ↔ calendar ↔ person at home instead of gym ↔ recurring payment.
beats.question: What happens when software applies the same model to ownership?
beats.reveal: The product is partly an intention, not just access.

beats.name: ADOBE RESET / OWNERSHIP
beats.vo: The gym did not invent the subscription trap. It industrialized the easiest version of it. And then software discovered it could do the same thing to something far more valuable than a treadmill: something you already owned. For about twenty years, buying software worked like buying an appliance: you bought the thing, then the transaction was over. You paid Adobe roughly seven hundred dollars for Photoshop. A box arrived. Inside was a disc and a licence key. The important part was not the box. It was the ending. The payment happened once, and the tool stayed with you.
beats.visual: Physical Photoshop CS6 box → disc → licence key → old purchase box next to modern subscription card.
beats.question: Why would a successful software company abandon one-time ownership?
beats.reveal: The economic relationship is about to change.

beats.name: ADOBE REVENUE PROBLEM
beats.vo: The problem, from Adobe's side, was the revenue chart. A new version shipped. Revenue spiked. People upgraded. Then the line flattened again while working copies stayed perfectly usable. By 2012, the software was good enough that the customer did not have to feel urgency every eighteen months. Your product can be excellent and your revenue can still wait.
beats.visual: Revenue sawtooth: release → spike → decay → release → spike; calendar advances while line flattens.
beats.question: What do you do when your best product is too good at being a one-time purchase?
beats.reveal: Adobe has a structural recurring-revenue problem.

beats.name: ADOBE DECISION
beats.vo: On May 6, 2013, Adobe announced that Creative Suite was finished. There would be no CS7. The forward path was Creative Cloud: a monthly subscription that continued as long as you kept paying.
beats.visual: May 6, 2013 date → Creative Suite box → BUY fades → SUBSCRIBE remains.
beats.question: What happens when customers hate the transition?
beats.reveal: Adobe has changed the ownership relationship.

beats.name: BACKLASH / THE CHOICE HOLDS
beats.vo: The reaction was furious. Petitions appeared. Professional designers argued that under the old model, if you stopped paying, you kept the tool. Under the new model, if you stopped paying, the software stopped being yours to use. Adobe did it anyway.
beats.visual: Forum posts → petition → designer hands → Adobe decision; backlash headlines on left, subscription path on right.
beats.question: Did the backlash actually stop the business model?
beats.reveal: Customer anger did not prevent the recurring model from succeeding.

beats.name: ADOBE NUMBERS / THE ECONOMIC MACHINE
beats.vo: Adobe's subscription revenue in 2013 was about one point two three billion dollars. By 2023 it was eighteen point two eight billion. By 2025, Adobe's total subscription revenue had reached about twenty-two point nine billion. The point is not that Photoshop became eighteen times better. It did not. The billing relationship changed more dramatically than the product did. A customer who might buy again became a customer who had to keep paying to retain access.
beats.visual: $1.23B → $18.28B → ~$22.9B. Keep each number isolated. Then BUY ONCE → KEEP PAYING diagram.
beats.question: What other consumer industry could rebuild itself this way?
beats.reveal: The revenue machine is larger than the product improvement.

beats.name: STREAMING RESET
beats.vo: The clearest proof that the model spread is not in software. It is in the thing that was supposed to destroy cable.
beats.visual: 2007 cable bill → early streaming interface → modern TV with multiple services.
beats.text: STREAMING WAS SUPPOSED TO ESCAPE CABLE
beats.question: Did streaming actually escape the subscription problem?
beats.reveal: A new chapter tests the same mechanism in entertainment.

beats.name: CABLE VS STREAMING PROMISE
beats.vo: For years, the argument against cable was the bundle. You paid one big monthly bill for hundreds of channels, watched a fraction of them, and had almost no way to buy exactly what you wanted. Streaming was sold as the escape. Pay for what you want. Cancel any time. No installer. No box. No giant cable package.
beats.visual: Cable bill with huge bundle → clean streaming card; each promise appears one at a time.
beats.question: Why did the escape become another bundle?
beats.reveal: The original streaming promise creates the benchmark for the reversal.

beats.name: THE CATALOGUE SPLITS
beats.vo: And for a while, it was. Then every studio realised that licensing its catalogue to someone else's platform could be worth less than owning the subscription relationship itself. The catalogue split. The show you wanted moved. Another service launched. Another payment appeared.
beats.visual: Netflix → Hulu → Prime → Disney+ → Max → Paramount+ → Peacock → Apple TV+. Each appears as one more recurring charge, not a logo celebration.
beats.question: What happens when many small charges replace one large bill?
beats.reveal: The bundle fragments into multiple recurring decisions.

beats.name: THE NEW BUNDLE
beats.vo: By the middle of the decade, the average household was carrying multiple streaming services at once. The exact bundle varies, but the structure is familiar: several smaller recurring charges replacing one large recurring charge. The industry rebuilt the bundle. Same monthly recurrence. Same habit. The difference is that the bill is fragmented. One large bill is something you fight. Six smaller bills are easier to ignore.
beats.visual: One CABLE card physically fractures into six smaller subscription cards; total visual area remains similar.
beats.text: ONE BIG BILL → MANY SMALL BILLS
beats.question: What becomes more valuable once everything is recurring?
beats.reveal: Fragmentation changes the psychology of noticing a bill.

beats.name: THE EXIT QUESTION
beats.vo: That is why the streaming story matters here. The subscription did not merely sell access. It changed the psychology of the bill. And once everything is a subscription, product quality is only half the game. The other half is what happens at the exit. Because recurring revenue is strongest when the payment is automatic — and weakest when the customer starts thinking about stopping.
beats.visual: Multiple recurring charges → cursor moves toward cancel → frame gradually simplifies around the word LEAVE.
beats.question: What happens when a customer actually tries to leave?
beats.reveal: The story pivots from acquisition to cancellation.

beats.name: AMAZON / ENROLLMENT
beats.vo: In 2023, the Federal Trade Commission sued Amazon. The allegations were not about the price of Prime. They were about enrollment and cancellation. The FTC alleged that Amazon designed parts of the Prime signup process so consumers could be enrolled without meaningfully understanding what had happened. And then came the cancellation flow.
beats.visual: Amazon Prime-style enrollment reconstruction. Bright primary action, subdued alternate path, cursor hesitation.
beats.question: What did the customer have to do to leave?
beats.reveal: The case centers on the design of the exit, not only the entry.

beats.name: THE CANCELLATION MAZE
beats.vo: Each page asked whether you were sure. Each offered a reason to stay. At several points the continuation button was visually weaker than the button that abandoned the cancellation.
beats.visual: Confirmation → benefits → pause → discount → confirmation again. The exit path visibly accumulates steps.
beats.question: How long can the exit path become before leaving stops feeling worth it?
beats.reveal: Cancellation can be delayed through design friction.

beats.name: ILIAD
beats.vo: And internally, according to the FTC case record, Amazon employees had a name for the sequence. Iliad. They named it after Homer's epic about a war that lasted ten years. The name is memorable because the mechanism is memorable. The customer is not physically trapped. They are procedurally delayed.
beats.visual: UI maze → black → ILIAD → old Homer volume / pages → exit remains visible in the distance.
beats.question: How much was this worth?
beats.reveal: The internal name makes the cancellation mechanism concrete and memorable.

beats.name: $2.5 BILLION
beats.vo: On September 25, 2025, Amazon settled the FTC case. Two point five billion dollars. One billion was a civil penalty. One and a half billion was refunds to consumers harmed by the alleged Prime enrollment practices. Amazon also agreed to stop the practices the order covered.
beats.visual: Source document → black → $2.5B alone → $1B + $1.5B = $2.5B.
beats.question: Is Amazon the only giant facing the exit problem?
beats.reveal: The scale of the regulatory response.

beats.name: ADOBE CANCELLATION CASE
beats.vo: Amazon was not alone. In 2024, the Department of Justice sued Adobe over subscription cancellation practices. The complaint alleged that an early termination fee could be buried where consumers would not see it clearly before subscribing. The fee could amount to fifty percent of the remaining contract value. In March 2026, the Justice Department announced a proposed one hundred and fifty million dollar resolution: seventy-five million in civil penalties and seventy-five million in free services for customers, plus new disclosure and cancellation protections.
beats.visual: Adobe cancellation screen → late fee field → $150M settlement split → comparison beside Amazon $2.5B.
beats.question: If regulators are acting, where is the broad rule?
beats.reveal: Different cases converge on the same exit-friction problem.

beats.name: THE RULE SHOULD SOLVE IT
beats.vo: Which raises the obvious question. If the penalties are this large, and the practice is this well documented, surely somebody finally wrote a rule. Somebody did. It was called Click-to-Cancel. The idea was almost aggressively simple: if you can start a subscription easily, you must be able to end it at least as easily. No phone call. No retention maze. No Iliad.
beats.visual: FTC building → policy document → signup three steps vs cancel three steps.
beats.question: Does the rule actually survive?
beats.reveal: The audience thinks the story has found its solution.

beats.name: THE RULE IS GONE
beats.vo: But companies and trade groups challenged the rule. And on July 8, 2025, the Eighth Circuit vacated the FTC's rule on procedural grounds. The rule existed. It was coming. And then it was gone.
beats.visual: Court opinion → calendar July 8, 2025 → RULE EXISTS → VACATED → GONE.
beats.text: THE RULE EXISTED. THEN IT WAS GONE.
beats.question: Why did the rule disappear?
beats.reveal: The expected solution is reversed.

beats.name: PROCEDURE
beats.vo: The court did not endorse deceptive subscription practices. It held that the FTC had failed to complete a required preliminary regulatory analysis of the rule's expected costs and benefits. Procedure killed the rule. And the timing is what makes it remarkable. The rule was vacated days before it was due to become enforceable.
beats.visual: Court text → required analysis highlighted → black field PROCEDURE → calendar counting toward effective date.
beats.question: What does that leave consumers with in 2026?
beats.reveal: The rule failed procedurally, not because the court approved the practice.

beats.name: CURRENT STATE
beats.vo: So in 2026, there is no federal Click-to-Cancel rule in effect in the United States. The FTC has started the rulemaking process again, and states have their own subscription laws, but the single nationwide rule is not in force. Which means the friction is still legal at the federal level in places where other laws do not prohibit it. The retention screens are legal. The six-page cancellation flow may still be legal. The plan that is easy to start on a phone and harder to end may still be legal.
beats.visual: 2025 RULE → VACATED → 2026 NEW PROCESS; map of state variation; cancellation flow remains visible.
beats.question: What does the whole story mean for the viewer?
beats.reveal: Exit friction remains a live design and legal issue.

beats.name: THE EMPTY GYM AGAIN
beats.vo: Not necessarily because a regulator approves of the design. But because the legal system has not finished writing the rule that would make the symmetry mandatory. Go back to where this started.
beats.visual: Same empty-gym composition returns exactly; visual temperature and framing match the opening.
beats.question: What did the empty gym mean when we first saw it?
beats.reveal: The story is ready to reinterpret its opening image.

beats.name: EMPTY GYM CALLBACK / SYSTEM
beats.vo: Twenty point eight million members. Two thousand eight hundred and ninety-six clubs. Hundreds of people can stand inside a location at once; millions more can be paying customers who are somewhere else. For most of economic history, a company made money by giving you something. If it stopped delivering, you stopped paying. That link was the discipline of the transaction.
beats.visual: Empty room; member count and club count return as restrained evidence overlays; no camera move.
beats.text: THE EMPTY ROOM WAS THE BUSINESS MODEL
beats.question: What changed when subscriptions removed the natural ending?
beats.reveal: The opening emptiness changes meaning: it is economically useful, not merely empty.

beats.name: THE SUBSCRIPTION BREAKS THE LINK
beats.vo: The subscription economy weakened that link. The payment continues automatically. And it keeps continuing until you take deliberate action to stop it — action the company has a financial reason to make slightly harder than you can be bothered with.
beats.visual: Bank statement returns; recurring payment continues while the cursor hesitates near cancel.
beats.question: What should the viewer do with that knowledge?
beats.reveal: The mechanism becomes a personal audit problem.

beats.name: THE $133 REFRAME
beats.vo: That is what the hundred-and-thirty-three-dollar gap is useful for seeing. It is not evidence that every person is wasting exactly $133. It is the measured gap between what a group of consumers thought their recurring charges were and what those charges added up to when itemized.
beats.visual: $86 → $219 → $133; survey qualifier appears as source-sized support text beneath.
beats.question: What is the one useful action now?
beats.reveal: Reframe the statistic without overclaiming it.

beats.name: THE BANKING AUDIT
beats.vo: So here is the only useful thing to do with any of this. Open your banking app. Search the last twelve months — not one month, twelve. Look for charges that repeat at the same amount or around the same date. Every one of those is a decision you made once and have been renewing silently ever since.
beats.visual: Banking app / statement; cursor scans twelve months; recurring charges are highlighted one by one without flashy animation.
beats.question: Which recurring decisions do you actually choose to keep?
beats.reveal: The viewer receives one concrete action instead of a generic CTA.

beats.name: FINAL CHOICE / HARD STOP
beats.vo: Some of them you will want to keep. That's fine. That is a choice. The point is that it should be a choice. Right now, for most people, it is just the last thing they agreed to — still running.
beats.visual: Cursor stops on one recurring charge → clean black → hard stop. No outro.
beats.text: A CHOICE, NOT A FORGOTTEN DECISION
beats.question: What is the real choice underneath the whole story?
beats.reveal: The viewer leaves with agency, not a sales CTA.
